title: Count the Rectangles of Ones

concept.title: Count the rectangles that end at each cell, reusing the count of the previous smaller bar
body: Count **all** rectangles that consist only of ones (a single cell is a rectangle). Group them by their **bottom-right corner**. Use the heights `heights[j]` of the consecutive ones above (including) each cell of the current row, as in the problem of the largest rectangle of ones.

Let `cnt[j]` be the number of rectangles of ones whose bottom-right corner is the cell in column `j` of the current row. Such a rectangle has some width `w` (it spans columns `j-w+1 .. j`) and any height up to the minimum of `heights` in that range. Find the nearest column `p` to the left with `heights[p] < heights[j]` (a **monotonic stack** gives it). For widths that reach to `p` or beyond, the minimum is no longer `heights[j]`, so the rectangles are the ones counted by `cnt[p]`. For the widths `1 .. j-p`, the minimum is `heights[j]`: they give `heights[j] * (j - p)` rectangles.
Rows are processed one after another, so the whole grid costs O(n * m).

statement: A grid has `n` rows and `m` columns of the characters `0` and `1`. Count the rectangles (submatrices) that contain only `1`. Different positions are different rectangles, and a single cell with `1` counts as one.
inputFormat: Each of the next `n` lines has `m` characters, `0` or `1`, without spaces.

examples.note: 7 single cells, 4 rectangles of size 1x2, 1 of size 1x3, 4 of size 2x1, 2 of size 3x1, 2 of size 2x2 and 1 of size 3x2: 21 in total.

hints: Group the rectangles by their bottom-right corner and process the grid row by row with heights.
For a cell, rectangles that are not wider than the distance to the nearest lower bar are limited by the height of the cell.
Wider rectangles were already counted at that lower bar: add its count.
